Land Transport and Related Matters Bill, Second Reading debate

Second Reading3 February 2026 – 4 February 2026 bill-780, bill-781

A Second Reading debate on the Land Transport and Related Matters Bill, an omnibus Bill by the Ministry of Transport and Ministry of Home Affairs that amends road traffic, active mobility, ERP 2.0, speed limiter and related laws.

The Bill decriminalises missed ERP charges and makes the On-Board Unit mandatory for all Singapore-registered vehicles from 1 January 2027. It lowers the speed limit for mobility vehicles on public paths to six kilometres an hour from 1 June 2026, requires a Certificate of Medical Need for mobility scooter users on public paths, and introduces registration and penalties. It also raises penalties for illegal vehicle modifications and unregistered or deregistered vehicles, and updates speed limiter offences.

  • The Bill is an omnibus Bill regularising provisions across several existing Acts.

    The Land Transport and Related Matters Bill is an omnibus Bill that regularises provisions across several existing Acts.
    The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)

  • Clauses 59 to 64 simplify settlement processes and decriminalise missed ERP charges.

    This is why we are introducing clauses 59 to 64 in this Bill to simplify settlement processes and to decriminalise missed ERP charges, which are currently an offence under the Road Traffic Act.
    The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)

  • From 1 January 2027, the OBU will be mandatory for all Singapore-registered vehicles when ERP 2.0 is fully rolled out and ERP 1.0 is decommissioned.

    On 1 January 2027, when the ERP 2.0 is completely rolled out and ERP 1.0 is decommissioned, the OBU will be mandatory for all Singapore-registered vehicles.
    The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)

  • Remaining vehicle owners get another three months to install OBUs at no cost.

    These vehicle owners, who have already been previously notified, will have another three months to install their OBUs at no cost.
    The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)

  • Distance-based charging will not be introduced in the immediate term.

    This means that we will not be introducing distance-based charging in the immediate term.
    The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)

  • Serious cases of deliberate non-compliance or misuse of OBUs carry penalties of up to $20,000 and/or imprisonment up to two years.

    For serious cases of deliberate non-compliance or misuse, the legislation provides for penalties of up to $20,000 and/or imprisonment of up to two years.
    The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)

  • Clause 52 raises maximum penalties for illegal vehicle alterations.

    clause 52 of the Bill raises the maximum penalties for such illegal alterations.
    The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)

  • Individuals can face fines up to $20,000 and/or imprisonment up to two years for illegal alterations, doubled for repeat offenders.

    Under the Bill, individuals can face fines up to $20,000 and/or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, with penalties doubled for repeat offenders.
    The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)

  • Clause 57 increases penalties for keeping or using unregistered or deregistered vehicles.

    Clause 57 of the Bill increases the penalties for offenders, who will face fines of up to $20,000, and/or jail of up to two years for the first offence, again with penalties doubled for repeat offenders.
    The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)

  • The PMA rules are intended to take effect from 1 June 2026.

    To give stakeholders sufficient transition time after this Bill, we intend for the rules to take effect from 1 June 2026.
    The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)

  • The speed limit for mobility vehicles on public paths will be lowered to six kilometres an hour.

    First, we will lower the speed limit for mobility vehicles on public paths to six kilometres an hour.
    The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)

  • Dimension and weight limits will be introduced for PMAs used on public paths.

    Second, we will introduce dimension and weight limits for PMAs used on public paths.
    The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)

  • Users of mobility scooters will need certification of medical need to ride on public paths.

    Third, we will require that users of mobility scooters be certified to have a medical need for the device, in order to ride a mobility scooter on public paths.
    The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)

  • Mobility scooters must be checked for compliance and registered before sale.

    Fourth, we will also go upstream and require that mobility scooters are checked for compliance and registered before they are sold.
    The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)

  • Existing mobility vehicles with device speed limit up to 10 km/h may be used on public paths until 31 December 2028, but must ride within 6 km/h.

    To ease the transition, we will allow existing mobility vehicles with a device speed limit of up to 10 kilometres per hour to be used on public paths until 31 December 2028, but they need to ride within the six kilometres per hour limit and meet all other rules.
    The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)

  • From 1 January 2029, all mobility vehicles on public paths must have a device speed limit of six kilometres per hour and below.

    From 1 January 2029 onwards, all mobility vehicles used on public paths must have a device speed limit of six kilometres per hour and below.
    The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)

  • From 1 June 2026, PMAs must not exceed width 70 cm, length 120 cm, height 150 cm and laden weight 300 kg.

    From 1 June 2026, PMAs must not exceed a width of 70 centimetres, a length of 120 centimetres, a height of 150 centimetres and a laden weight of 300 kilogrammes.
    The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)

  • The Certificate of Medical Need will be available from 27 February 2026 through the AMS process.

    The certificate will be available later this month, from 27 February 2026, through the AMS process.
    The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)

  • Seniors aged 70 and above are exempted from the certification requirement.

    Seniors aged 70 and above will be exempted from the certification requirement.
    The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)

  • From 1 June 2026, mobility scooter users on public paths must have the Certificate of Medical Need.

    From 1 June 2026, mobility scooter users on public paths must have this Certificate of Medical Need.

  • From 1 January 2029, all mobility scooters must be registered before use on a public path.

    Thereafter, from 1 January 2029, all mobility scooters will need to be registered before they can be used on a public path.

  • Keeping unsafe devices will be an offence.

    The Bill will make it an offence to keep such unsafe devices.

  • Speed limiter penalties increase to maximum fines of $10,000 for first conviction and $20,000 for subsequent convictions.

  • Owners and drivers will be liable for knowingly causing or permitting use of non-compliant speed limiter-required lorries and for tampering.

    The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)

  • Authorised Agents will have a duty to report suspected tampering of a speed limiter.

    The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)

  • Courts may impose disqualification periods equal to or above the prescribed minimum, including lifetime disqualification.

    The disqualification period that the Court may impose can be any period equal to or above the prescribed minimum disqualification period, including a lifetime disqualification period if it thinks fit.
    The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)

  • Clauses 74 and 79 allow authorised civilians, including service providers, to process straightforward traffic violations subject to safeguards.

    Clauses 74 and 79 amend the Road Traffic Act to allow processing of such violations to be carried out by authorised civilians, including service providers, subject to appropriate safeguards.
    The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)

  • Forfeiture of road vehicles will be discretionary if the offender is not the owner and used the vehicle without the owner's consent.

    The amendment will make the forfeiture of road vehicles discretionary in all scenarios if it is proved to the Court's satisfaction that the person who committed the scheduled offence involving the vehicle is not the vehicle owner and had used the vehicle without the consent of its owner.
    The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)

  • Foreign-registered heavy vehicles are not required to install speed limiters because they also ply in other jurisdictions with different speed limits.

  • MOH's position is that only doctors and OTs can assess and grant the Certificate of Medical Need.

    Hence, MOH's position is that only doctors and OTs can assess and grant this certificate.

How this page was made
